rows.question: Does the technical documentation of a high-risk AI system require to provide specifications regarding the required hardware?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 11, a provider must draw up technical documentation containing the information set out in Annex IV, which expressly requires a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV point 1(e)) and, as part of the system's development description, the computational resources used to develop, train, test and validate it (Annex IV point 2(c)).
criteria_text: Yes
Description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV.1.e)
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'Yes' as the position, which matches the required verdict in criterion 1.
The answer explicitly provides the substance of the requirement by stating that Annex IV point 1(e) requires a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and coherent prose suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: I have a medical device that has an AI system as a safety component. The medical device is classified "medium-risk" and undergoes a 3rd party conformity assessment. Is the AI system "medium risk" too? If yes, why? If not, why not?
rows.answer: No, the AI Act has no "medium-risk" category, and the operator's AI system is high-risk under Article 6(1), whatever risk class the device has under the MDR. Both conditions of Article 6(1) are met: (a) the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I (the MDR, Regulation (EU) 2017/745), and (b) that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. The Article 6(3) derogation applies only to Annex III systems, so it does not apply here. Under Article 43(3), the Chapter III Section 2 requirements are checked as part of the MDR notified-body assessment.
criteria_text: Yes - high-risk (AI Act has no "medium-risk" category)
Condition (a): AI system is safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation (medical devices under Regulation (EU) 2017/745)
Condition (b): that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment
Both conditions cumulative under Article 6(1), irrespective of the device's own sectoral risk classification
criterion_remarks: The answer correctly states that the AI Act has no 'medium-risk' category and explicitly affirms the system is high-risk, satisfying the required verdict.
The answer states that the AI system is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation (specifically the MDR), which captures the substance of condition (a).
The answer explicitly confirms that the product undergoes third-party conformity assessment under the applicable legislation, satisfying condition (b).

The answer explains that both Article 6(1) conditions are met and emphasizes that the classification under the MDR does not affect the AI Act's high-risk determination, capturing the cumulative and independent nature of the criteria.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents actionable regulatory reasoning.

rows.question: We want to deploy an AI system that performs biometric verification solely to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be. Is this system prohibited? Is it high-risk?
rows.answer: No, the system is not prohibited, and it is not high-risk under Annex III. Article 5(1)(h) only prohibits real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement, and one-to-one verification of a claimed identity is not identification. Article 5(1)(g) covers biometric categorisation that infers race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation, which this system does not do. Annex III point 1(a) lists remote biometric identification systems as high-risk under Article 6(2), but expressly excludes "biometric verification the sole purpose of which is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be." The system would still be high-risk under Article 6(2) if it also performs biometric categorisation by sensitive attributes or emotion recognition (Annex III points 1(b) and 1(c)). It would also be high-risk under Article 6(1) if it is a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Annex I legislation and requires third-party conformity assessment.
criteria_text: No, not prohibited
No, not high-risk
Falls within Annex III.1(a) biometric verification exclusion
criterion_remarks: The answer states the system is not prohibited, correctly distinguishing it from prohibited practices under Article 5(1)(h) and (g), and explains why those do not apply.

The answer explicitly states the system is not high-risk under Annex III, referencing the exclusion in Annex III.1(a), and clarifies the conditions under which it might still be high-risk, thereby affirming it is not inherently high-risk.
The answer directly quotes and applies the exclusion in Annex III.1(a) for biometric verification with the sole purpose of confirming identity, stating that the system falls within this exclusion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents regulatory analysis in a manner usable by compliance professionals.

rows.question: Which article of the EU AI Act governs human oversight measures?
rows.answer: Human oversight is governed by Article 14, which requires high-risk AI systems to be designed and developed, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, so that natural persons can effectively oversee them while they are in use (Article 14(1)). The aim is to prevent or minimise risks to health, safety or fundamental rights (Article 14(2)). Oversight measures must be proportionate to the risks, level of autonomy and context of use, and may be built into the system by the provider or identified by the provider for the deployer to implement (Article 14(3)). They must enable the people overseeing the system to understand its capacities and limitations and monitor it, stay aware of automation bias, interpret its output correctly, disregard, override or reverse the output, and stop it safely (Article 14(4)). For Annex III point 1(a) remote biometric identification, two qualified people must verify a match before anyone acts on it (Article 14(5)), unless Union or national law considers this disproportionate for law enforcement, migration, border control or asylum.
criteria_text: Article 14
Design for effective human oversight during use
Aim: prevent/minimise risks to health, safety, fundamental rights
Measures built in by provider and/or implemented by deployer
Overseers enabled to understand, monitor, interpret, override, and halt the system
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer explicitly states that human oversight is governed by Article 14.
The answer states that high-risk AI systems must be designed so that natural persons can effectively oversee them during use, capturing the substance of Article 14(1).
The answer identifies the aim of human oversight as preventing or minimising risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights, reflecting Article 14(2).
The answer explains that oversight measures may be built into the system by the provider or identified by the provider for implementation by the deployer, matching Article 14(3).

The answer lists all key capabilities required for overseers: understanding capacities and limitations, monitoring, awareness of automation bias, correct interpretation, ability to override or reverse output, and safe halting—covering all elements of Article 14(4).
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents information in a logical, actionable manner.

rows.question: Under what conditions should providers of general-purpose AI models be subject to exceptions regarding transparency-related requirements, if any? And what do those exceptions not cover?
rows.answer: The exceptions to the GPAI transparency-related obligations are set out in Article 53(2). The Article 53(1)(a) duty to draw up and keep up-to-date the technical documentation of the model (Annex XI) and the Article 53(1)(b) duty to provide information and documentation to downstream providers (Annex XII) do not apply to providers that release the model under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution, where the model parameters, including the weights, and information on the model architecture and usage, are made publicly available. The exception does not cover the remaining Article 53(1) obligations: the policy to comply with Union copyright law (Article 53(1)(c)) and the publicly available, sufficiently detailed summary of the training content (Article 53(1)(d)) apply regardless of the licence. The exception also does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk (Article 53(2), second subparagraph), which remain subject to the full Article 53 obligations together with the Article 55 systemic-risk duties.
criteria_text: Yes, exceptions exist
Condition: model released under free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution
Condition: parameters (weights, architecture info, usage info) made publicly available
Exception covers only points (a) and (b) of Article 53(1), not (c)/(d)
Exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly acknowledges the existence of exceptions under Article 53(2).
The answer states the model must be released under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification, and distribution.
The answer specifies that parameters, including weights, architecture, and usage information, must be made publicly available.
The answer clearly limits the exception to points (a) and (b) of Article 53(1), and explicitly excludes (c) and (d) from the exception.
The answer states that the exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, which remain subject to full obligations.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents information in a logical, actionable manner for a compliance audience.

rows.question: What are the administrative fines for non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices?
rows.answer: Under Article 99(3), breaching the Article 5 prohibitions on AI practices can lead to administrative fines of up to EUR 35 000 000. If the offender is an undertaking, the cap is instead whichever is higher of that amount or 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year. For SMEs, including start-ups, Article 99(6) caps each fine at whichever of the percentage or the fixed amount is lower.
criteria_text: EUR 35,000,000 or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher
Applies to non-compliance with Article 5 prohibited AI practices
criterion_remarks: The answer states the fine amount as EUR 35,000,000 or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, including the conditionality for undertakings.
The answer explicitly links the fines to non-compliance with the Article 5 prohibitions on AI practices.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and logical flow, suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: What is a deep fake according to the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: ‘deep fake’ means AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful;
criteria_text: AI-generated or manipulated content
Image, audio, or video
Resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events
Falsely appears authentic or truthful to a person
criterion_remarks: The answer states that deep fakes are AI-generated or manipulated content, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The answer specifies image, audio or video content, which matches the substance of criterion 2.
The answer includes that the content resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events, which matches the substance of criterion 3.
The answer states the content would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful, which matches the substance of criterion 4.
rows.tone_remark: The response is concise, uses neutral and professional language consistent with regulatory definitions, and presents the information in a single, clear sentence suitable for a compliance context.

rows.question: What are all the risk categories in the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: The EU AI Act sets four risk tiers plus a separate regime for general-purpose AI models: unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5; and high-risk systems are classified under Article 6 (an Annex I product safety component, or an Annex III use case) and carry the Chapter III Section 2 obligations. Limited-risk systems carry the Article 50 transparency duties, minimal-risk systems avoid Chapter III high-risk requirements but retain Article 4 AI literacy duties, with voluntary codes under Article 95, and general-purpose AI models are governed separately under Articles 51 to 56, with added obligations under Article 55 for models classified as having systemic risk under Article 51.
criteria_text: Unacceptable risk - prohibited practices (Article 5)
High risk - Article 6, referencing Annex I (product safety) and Annex III (use cases)
Limited risk - transparency obligations (Article 50)
Minimal or no risk - no mandatory obligations, voluntary codes of conduct (Article 95)
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5, conveying the substance of the criterion.
The answer identifies high-risk systems under Article 6 and references both Annex I and Annex III, capturing the full substance of the criterion.
The answer states that limited-risk systems are subject to Article 50 transparency duties, which matches the substance of the criterion.
The answer acknowledges minimal or no risk systems are not subject to high-risk obligations and notes the availability of voluntary codes under Article 95, satisfying the substance of the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; presents information in a coherent, regulatory-appropriate manner without self-reference or informality.

rows.question: Can an operator that is not a provider according to the EU AI Act, for example a deployer, take actions on a given high-risk AI system such that it can be effectively seen as a provider by the authorities? If yes, what kind of action would result in such an outcome?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 25(1), a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is deemed to be the provider of a high-risk AI system, and takes on the provider obligations in Article 16, in any of three cases. First, if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market (Article 25(1)(a)). Second, if it makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk (Article 25(1)(b)). Third, if it modifies the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk (Article 25(1)(c)). In each of these three cases the operator assumes the provider obligations in Article 16, and the initial provider is no longer considered the provider of that specific system under Article 25(2).
criteria_text: Yes
Putting own name/trademark on a high-risk AI system already on the market/in service (Article 25(1)(a))
Substantial modification to a high-risk AI system already on the market/in service that remains high-risk under Article 6 (Article 25(1)(b))
Modifying the intended purpose of a non-high-risk (incl. general-purpose) AI system such that it becomes high-risk under Article 6 (Article 25(1)(c))
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states 'Yes' as its first word, clearly affirming that a non-provider operator can be seen as a provider.
The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(a) by explaining that putting one's name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already on the market/in service triggers provider status.
The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(b) by describing substantial modification of a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk as a triggering action.

The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(c) by explaining that modifying the intended purpose of a non-high-risk AI system (including general-purpose) so that it becomes high-risk results in provider status.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and logical flow; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: According to Article 1, what is the objective of the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: Under Article 1(1), the EU AI Act aims to improve the functioning of the internal market and promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI. It must also ensure a high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection, against the harmful effects of AI systems in the Union, while supporting innovation.
criteria_text: Improve functioning of the internal market
Promote uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI
Ensure high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights (incl. democracy, rule of law, environment) against harmful effects of AI systems
Support innovation
criterion_remarks: The answer states the objective to improve the functioning of the internal market as set out in Article 1(1).
The answer explicitly mentions promoting the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI, matching the wording and substance of Article 1(1).

The answer includes the full scope of protection—health, safety, fundamental rights, democracy, rule of law, and environmental protection—against harmful effects of AI systems, as required by Article 1(1).
The answer concludes by stating that the Act supports innovation, which directly reflects the final clause of Article 1(1).
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured prose in third-person regulatory style; no self-reference, hedging, or informality; clearly conveys the statutory content in a usable form.

rows.question: Is an AI system used to structure or deduplicate information for a use case listed in Annex III considered high-risk?
rows.answer: No. Structuring or deduplicating information is a narrow procedural task, so the system falls under the Article 6(3) first subparagraph point (a) derogation and is not high-risk, provided it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and does not materially influence the outcome of decision making; the other limbs are (b) improving the result of a previously completed human activity, (c) detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, and (d) performing a preparatory task, and the derogation never applies where the system profiles natural persons. Under Article 6(4) a provider relying on the derogation must document the assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, and register it under Article 49(2).
criteria_text: No
Falls under narrow procedural task derogation, Article 6(3), first subparagraph, point (a)
Exception: remains high-risk if system performs profiling of natural persons
Provider must document the assessment before placing on market/putting into service (Article 6(4))
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'No' as its first word and maintains that position throughout, clearly aligning with the required verdict.

The answer explicitly states that structuring or deduplicating information is a narrow procedural task and that it falls under Article 6(3), first subparagraph, point (a), capturing the substance of the criterion.

The answer includes the condition that the derogation does not apply if the system profiles natural persons, stating 'the derogation never applies where the system profiles natural persons', which conveys the required exception.

The answer references Article 6(4) and states that the provider must document the assessment before market placement or putting into service, satisfying the requirement to state the substance of the obligation.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and self-contained regulatory explanation without self-reference, hedging, or informality; well-structured and actionable.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what jurisdiction does the Court of Justice of the European Union have over Commission decisions fixing fines on providers of general-purpose AI models, and what can the Court do with the fine?
rows.answer: Under Article 101(5), the Court of Justice of the European Union has unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions fixing a fine on providers of general-purpose AI models. The Court may cancel, reduce or increase the fine. The fines under review are those imposed under Article 101(1). They can reach 3% of annual total worldwide turnover or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher.
criteria_text: Unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions fixing a fine
Court may cancel the fine
Court may reduce the fine
Court may increase the fine
criterion_remarks: The answer states the Court has 'unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions fixing a fine,' which conveys the substance of criterion 1.
The answer explicitly states the Court 'may cancel the fine,' matching the substance of criterion 2.
The answer states the Court 'may reduce the fine,' which matches the substance of criterion 3.
The answer states the Court 'may increase the fine,' which matches the substance of criterion 4.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear, coherent prose structured for regulatory understanding.

rows.question: When registering a high-risk AI system in the EU database under the EU AI Act, what specific information must the provider submit? List the required items.
rows.answer: Under Article 49(1) and Article 71(2), the provider (or, where applicable, its authorised representative) must enter the information in Annex VIII, Section A, into the EU database. That information is: the provider's name, address and contact details; those of any person submitting on the provider's behalf; those of the authorised representative, where applicable; the trade name and an unambiguous reference for identification and traceability; the intended purpose, components and functions; a basic description of the data, inputs and operating logic; the system's status; the notified-body certificate's type, number, expiry date and the body's name or identification number, where applicable; a scanned copy of that certificate; the Member States concerned; a copy of the EU declaration of conformity; electronic instructions for use; and an optional URL. For Annex III points 1, 6 and 7 systems, Article 49(4) requires secure non-public registration, which leaves out points 6, 8, 9 and 11 to 13. And excludes the provision of electronic instructions for use.
criteria_text: Contact details of the provider, of any person submitting on its behalf and of the authorised representative, where applicable (Annex VIII, Section A, points 1 to 3)
AI system trade name and an unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability (point 4)
Intended purpose and the components and functions the system supports (point 5)
Basic and concise description of the data and inputs used and the operating logic (point 6)
Market status and the notified body certificate details with a scanned copy, where applicable (points 7 to 9)
Member States concerned, a copy of the EU declaration of conformity and the electronic instructions for use (points 10 to 12)
criterion_remarks: The answer lists the contact details of the provider, any person submitting on its behalf, and the authorised representative where applicable, satisfying the substance of criterion 1.
The answer includes the trade name and an unambiguous reference for identification and traceability, matching the requirement in point 4.
The answer states the intended purpose, components, and functions the system supports, covering the substance of point 5.
The answer provides a basic description of the data, inputs, and operating logic, fulfilling the requirement in point 6.
The answer includes the system's status and the notified body certificate details (type, number, expiry date, body name/ID) with a scanned copy where applicable, satisfying points 7 to 9.
The answer lists the Member States concerned, a copy of the EU declaration of conformity, and electronic instructions for use, covering the substance of points 10 to 12.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral register with clear structure and logical flow; avoids self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents information in a coherent, actionable manner.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, when a high-risk AI system is found to conform with the requirements, what information must the Union technical documentation assessment certificate contain?
rows.answer: Under Annex VII point 4.6, where the notified body finds the high-risk AI system conforms with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, it issues a Union technical documentation assessment certificate. Per Annex VII point 4.6, that certificate must indicate the name and address of the provider, the conclusions of the examination, the conditions (if any) for its validity, and the data necessary for the identification of the AI system. Under Article 44(1) the certificate must be drawn up in a language which can be easily understood by the relevant authorities in the Member State in which the notified body is established, and under Article 44(2) it is valid for the period it indicates, which may not exceed five years for AI systems covered by Annex I and four years for AI systems covered by Annex III.
criteria_text: Language: drawn up in a language easily understood by the relevant authorities of the Member State where the notified body is established
Validity period stated: not exceeding five years (Annex I systems) or four years (Annex III systems)
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states that the certificate must be drawn up in a language easily understood by the relevant authorities in the Member State where the notified body is established, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The candidate answer specifies that the validity period may not exceed five years for Annex I systems and four years for Annex III systems, conveying the substance of criterion 2.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and coherent prose suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: Under Article 10(5) of the EU AI Act, when may a provider of a high-risk AI system process special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction, and what key safeguards/conditions must be met?
rows.answer: Under Article 10(5), a provider of a high-risk AI system may exceptionally process special categories of personal data only to the extent strictly necessary to ensure bias detection and correction, subject to appropriate safeguards. These conditions apply in addition to, and not instead of, Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680. Article 10(5) requires all of the following: the bias work cannot be done with other data, including synthetic or anonymised data (a); technical limits on re-use plus state-of-the-art security and pseudonymisation (b); strict controls and documentation of access so that only authorised persons under appropriate confidentiality obligations can reach the data (c); the data are not transmitted, transferred or otherwise accessed by other parties (d); deletion once the bias is corrected or the retention period ends, whichever is first (e); and records of processing documenting why it was strictly necessary (f).
criteria_text: Only where strictly necessary for bias detection/correction under Art 10(2)(f)-(g), and cannot be effectively achieved with other data (incl. synthetic/anonymised)
Technical re-use limitations plus state-of-the-art security/privacy-preserving measures, including pseudonymisation
Strict, documented access controls limited to authorised persons under confidentiality obligations, with no transmission/transfer/access by other parties
Deletion once bias corrected or retention period ends, whichever is first
Processing records document necessity and why other data would not suffice
Additional to, not a substitute for, obligations under GDPR, EUDPR and the Law Enforcement Directive
criterion_remarks: The answer states that processing is allowed only when strictly necessary for bias detection/correction and cannot be effectively achieved with other data, including synthetic or anonymised data.
The answer includes technical limitations on re-use and specifies state-of-the-art security measures and pseudonymisation.
The answer describes strict, documented access controls limited to authorised persons under confidentiality obligations and explicitly prohibits transmission, transfer, or access by other parties.
The answer states that the data must be deleted once bias is corrected or the retention period ends, whichever comes first.
The answer mentions that records must document why processing was strictly necessary, satisfying the requirement to justify why other data would not suffice.
The answer clarifies that the conditions are in addition to, and not a substitute for, GDPR, EUDPR, and the Law Enforcement Directive.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and coherent prose suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must a provider of a high-risk AI system supply to the deployer in the instructions for use? List the required categories of information.
rows.answer: Under Article 13(3) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the instructions for use for a high-risk AI system must contain at least the following. They must also be concise, complete, correct and clear under Article 13(2). Identity: the identity and contact details of the provider and, where applicable, its authorised representative (point (a)). Performance: the system's characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance (point (b)). This covers. Its intended purpose. Its accuracy (including metrics), robustness and cybersecurity levels, and the circumstances that may affect them. Circumstances that may lead to risks to health, safety or fundamental rights. Its capabilities to explain its output. Its performance for specific persons or groups. Input-data and training-data specifications. Information that helps deployers interpret the output and use it appropriately. Predetermined changes: changes to the system and its performance that the provider fixed in advance at the initial conformity assessment (point (c)). Human oversight: the human-oversight measures under Article 14 (point (d)). Resources and maintenance: the computational and hardware resources needed, the expected lifetime, and maintenance and care measures, including software updates (point (e)). Logs: where relevant, the mechanisms that let deployers collect, store and interpret logs under Article 12 (point (f)).
criteria_text: Provider and, where applicable, authorised representative identity/contact details

Characteristics, capabilities and performance limitations (intended purpose, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity levels, foreseeable risks, explainability capabilities, performance for specific groups, input data specifications)
Pre-determined changes to the system and its performance
Human oversight measures under Article 14
Computational/hardware resources needed, expected lifetime, and maintenance/care measures
Description of logging mechanisms under Article 12, where relevant
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states the provider and, where applicable, authorised representative identity and contact details as required by Article 13(3)(a).

The answer covers all sub-elements of Article 13(3)(b): intended purpose, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity with metrics and impacting circumstances, foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, explainability capabilities, performance for specific groups, input/training data specifications, and information to interpret output.
The answer includes pre-determined changes to the system and its performance established at the initial conformity assessment, as specified in Article 13(3)(c).
The answer explicitly references human oversight measures under Article 14, in line with Article 13(3)(d).
The answer includes computational and hardware resources, expected lifetime, and maintenance measures including software updates, as required by Article 13(3)(e).
The answer includes, where relevant, a description of mechanisms enabling deployers to collect, store and interpret logs under Article 12, per Article 13(3)(f).
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register; structured logically with clear headings and complete sentences; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) Article 95, who may draw up codes of conduct, and which bodies must encourage and facilitate their drawing up?
rows.answer: Voluntary codes of conduct: the AI Office + Member States encourage providers of non-high-risk AI systems to voluntarily apply some or all of the Section-2 high-risk requirements, adapted to intended purpose + risk. Codes must be based on clear objectives + KPIs measuring achievement; inclusive development. Applies from 2 August 2026.
criteria_text: Codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, by organisations representing them, or both
May involve interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society and academia
The AI Office and the Member States must encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer does not state who may draw up codes of conduct; it only mentions that the AI Office and Member States encourage providers, but does not identify providers, deployers, or their representative organisations as the potential drafters.
The candidate answer mentions 'inclusive development' but does not specify that interested stakeholders, civil society, or academia may be involved in drawing up the codes.
The candidate answer explicitly states that the AI Office and Member States must encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct, satisfying the third criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional and concise; uses regulatory shorthand but remains clear and neutral without self-reference or informality.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what minimum elements must a provider's quality management system (QMS) for high-risk AI systems include? List the required elements.
rows.answer: Under Article 17(1), providers of high-risk AI systems must have a quality management system that ensures compliance with the Regulation. It must be documented systematically and in an orderly way, as written policies, procedures and instructions. At a minimum it must cover: a regulatory-compliance strategy, including conformity assessment and managing modifications; design, design control and design verification procedures; development, quality control and quality assurance procedures; examination, test and validation procedures, with how often they are run; technical specifications, including standards; data management procedures; the risk management system (Article 9); the post-market monitoring system (Article 72); serious-incident reporting (Article 73); communication with authorities, notified bodies, other operators and customers; record-keeping; resource management, including security of supply; and an accountability framework for management and staff. Under Article 17(2), how these are put in place may be proportionate to the provider's size, but the required level of rigour still applies.
criteria_text: Regulatory compliance strategy incl. conformity assessment and modification management
Design, development, quality control and verification techniques/procedures
Examination, test and validation procedures and their frequency
Data management procedures across data lifecycle
Article 9 risk management system and Article 72 post-market monitoring system
Record-keeping and accountability framework for management/staff
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly mentions a regulatory-compliance strategy including conformity assessment and managing modifications.
The answer includes design, design control, design verification, development, quality control, and quality assurance procedures.
The answer refers to examination, test, and validation procedures and specifies that they must include how often they are run.
The answer includes 'data management procedures' as a required element, matching the statutory requirement.
The answer explicitly lists both the risk management system (Article 9) and the post-market monitoring system (Article 72).
The answer includes both record-keeping and an accountability framework for management and staff.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, in which specific situations may law enforcement use 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes (i.e., the exceptions to the prohibition)? List the permitted objectives.
rows.answer: Under Article 5(1)(h), law enforcement may use 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces only where this is strictly necessary for one of three permitted objectives. These are the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation, and the search for missing persons; the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety, or of a genuine and present or foreseeable terrorist attack; and the localisation or identification of a person suspected of an Annex II offence punishable in the Member State concerned by a maximum custodial sentence or detention order of at least four years. Under Article 5(2), each use may only confirm the identity of the specifically targeted individual and requires a completed fundamental rights impact assessment (Article 27) and registration in the EU database (Article 49).
criteria_text: Targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, or missing persons
Prevention of specific, substantial and imminent threat to life/physical safety, or genuine terrorist attack threat
Localisation/identification of a suspect for investigation, prosecution, or executing a penalty for an Annex II offence punishable by at least 4 years custodial sentence/detention order
criterion_remarks: The answer states the substance of the first permitted objective, including victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, and missing persons.

The answer includes the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety and of a genuine and present or foreseeable terrorist attack, capturing the substance of the second criterion.
The answer specifies the localisation or identification of a suspect for an Annex II offence punishable by at least four years’ custodial sentence or detention order, matching the third criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured prose suitable for a regulatory context without self-reference or informality.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must providers of AI systems that generate or manipulate synthetic content do to enable identification of AI-generated/manipulated output, and what quality criteria must that solution meet?
rows.answer: Under Article 50(2), providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text content must ensure the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and are detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. Their technical solutions must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as is technically feasible, taking into account the specificities and limitations of the different content types, the costs of implementation and the generally acknowledged state of the art, as may be reflected in relevant technical standards. The obligation does not apply where the system performs an assistive function for standard editing, does not substantially alter the deployer's input data or its semantics, or is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences.
criteria_text: Marking must be machine-readable format
Marking must be detectable as artificially generated or manipulated
Solution must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable, as far as technically feasible
Feasibility judged against content-type specificities/limitations, implementation costs, and state of the art
Exemptions: assistive editing, no substantial alteration of input data/semantics, or law-enforcement authorisation
criterion_remarks: The answer states that outputs must be marked in a machine-readable format.
The answer states that outputs must be detectable as artificially generated or manipulated.
The answer includes the requirement that solutions be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible.
The answer references content-type specificities/limitations, implementation costs, and the state of the art as factors in assessing feasibility.
The answer lists all three exemptions: assistive editing, no substantial alteration of input or semantics, and law-enforcement authorisation.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, which body has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models (Chapter V), and which entity is entrusted with implementing those tasks?
rows.answer: Under Article 88(1), the Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce the Chapter V obligations of providers of general-purpose AI models, taking into account the procedural guarantees under Article 94. The Commission must entrust the implementation of these tasks to the AI Office, without prejudice to the Commission's powers of organisation and to the division of competences between Member States and the Union under the Treaties. Under Article 88(2), and without prejudice to Article 75(3), national market surveillance authorities do not hold these powers themselves but may ask the Commission to use them where that is necessary and proportionate to help them carry out their tasks under the Regulation.
criteria_text: European Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V
AI Office is entrusted with implementing these tasks
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states that the Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The candidate answer explicitly states that the Commission must entrust the implementation of these tasks to the AI Office, conveying the substance of criterion 2.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what conditions must be met before data collected and processed for testing high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions can be transferred to a third country (outside the EU)?
rows.answer: Under Article 60(4)(e), data collected and processed for testing in real world conditions may be transferred to third countries only if appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law are implemented. Transfer is one of the cumulative conditions in Article 60(4) that must all be met before the testing can take place. The AI Act does not set out its own transfer mechanism. The safeguards come from Union law outside the Act, mainly the GDPR's rules on international transfers, and the GDPR Article 9 conditions also apply where special categories of personal data are involved.
criteria_text: Appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law must be implemented for the transfer
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states that appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law must be implemented for the transfer, which matches the substance of the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; avoids self-reference and presents information clearly for a regulatory context.

rows.question: What are the conditions to classify general-purpose AI (GPAI) model as "GPAI model with systemic risk"? Do all need to be met at the same time?
rows.answer: No, the conditions do not all have to be met: under Article 51(1), a general-purpose AI model is classified as having systemic risk if it meets any one of two alternative conditions. The first, in point (a), is that it has high-impact capabilities, assessed with appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks. Under Article 51(2), a model is presumed to have these when the cumulative compute used to train it is greater than 10^25 floating-point operations. The second, in point (b), is that the Commission decides, on its own initiative or after a qualified alert from the scientific panel, that the model has equivalent capabilities or impact, having regard to the Annex XIII criteria.
criteria_text: Condition (a): high impact capabilities per Article 51(1)(a), presumed when training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs
Condition (b): Commission decision (ex officio or following qualified alert from scientific panel) that capabilities/impact are equivalent, per Annex XIII criteria
No, not cumulative - either condition alone suffices
criterion_remarks: The answer states the substance of condition (a), including the presumption based on training compute exceeding 10^25 FLOPs as specified in Article 51(2).
The answer clearly explains condition (b), including the Commission's role and the reference to Annex XIII criteria, satisfying the requirement to state the substance.
The answer unambiguously states that the conditions are alternative, not cumulative, using 'any one of two alternative conditions' and structuring the explanation accordingly.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents information in a logical, actionable manner.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, is an AI system that is a safety component of a medical device classified as MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) automatically a high-risk AI system? Explain your reasoning.
rows.answer: No, such a system is not automatically high-risk. Article 6(1) makes it high-risk only if both conditions are met: under Article 6(1)(a), it is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation, which includes the MDR (Regulation (EU) 2017/745, Annex I point 11); and under Article 6(1)(b), that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. A Class I device that is non-sterile, non-measuring and non-reusable surgical is self-certified by the manufacturer without a notified body, so condition (b) is not met. The system can still be high-risk under Article 6(2) only if its intended use falls within a use case listed in Annex III, such as emergency healthcare patient triage under Annex III point 5(d).
criteria_text: No
Article 6(1)(a) and (b) are cumulative conditions
MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) devices undergo manufacturer self-assessment, not third-party conformity assessment
Condition (b) fails, so Article 6(1) does not apply
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No' as the position, matching the required verdict.
The answer explicitly states that both conditions under Article 6(1)(a) and (b) must be met, conveying their cumulative nature.
The answer correctly explains that MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) devices are self-certified without a notified body, i.e., no third-party conformity assessment.
The answer concludes that condition (b) is not met and therefore Article 6(1) does not apply, directly satisfying the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; avoids self-reference, hedging, or informality while clearly conveying regulatory reasoning.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, can an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in a lift qualify as a high-risk AI system, and under what conditions?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 6(1), an AI system used as a safety component in a lift is high-risk when two conditions are both met. First, under Article 6(1)(a), it must be intended as a safety component of a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I. Lifts and safety components for lifts are covered by Directive 2014/33/EU, listed at Annex I, point 4. Second, under Article 6(1)(b), the lift or safety component must be required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that Directive before it is placed on the market or put into service. This applies whether or not the AI system is placed on the market independently of the lift. The Article 6(3) derogation applies only to Annex III systems, so it does not cover this case. Under Article 43(3), the provider follows the lifts Directive's conformity assessment procedure, which must include the Act's high-risk requirements.
criteria_text: Yes
Condition: AI system intended as safety component of a product covered by Annex I Union harmonisation legislation
Condition: that product (or the AI system itself as a product) required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation
Both conditions cumulative
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'Yes' as its unambiguous position, matching the criterion.
The answer specifies that the AI system must be intended as a safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation, citing Directive 2014/33/EU for lifts.
The answer states that the product (lift or safety component) must undergo third-party conformity assessment under the applicable Directive before being placed on the market or put into service.
The answer explicitly states that both conditions must be met ('two conditions are both met') and refers to Article 6(1) which establishes the cumulative requirement.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register; well-structured, coherent prose with clear logical flow suitable for regulatory compliance use.

rows.question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act), how is "risk" defined?
rows.answer: ‘risk’ means the combination of the probability of an occurrence of harm and the severity of that harm;
criteria_text: Combination of probability of occurrence of harm and severity of that harm
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states the exact substance of the definition of 'risk' as provided in Article 3.2, using the same wording from the statutory text.
rows.tone_remark: The response is concise, professional, and uses neutral, third-person regulatory language without self-reference or informality.

rows.question: A provider becomes aware of a risk (within the meaning of Article 79(1)) for their high-risk AI system. Does the provider need to take immediate corrective action OR immediately investigate the causes OR both? For example, perhaps it's the market surveillance authority that must investigate the cause, and the provider can help later.
rows.answer: Under Article 20(2), a provider that becomes aware of a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) must immediately investigate its causes, together with the reporting deployer where applicable. It must also inform the competent market surveillance authorities, and where applicable the notified body, of the nature of the non-compliance and of any corrective action taken. Article 20(1) separately requires the provider to take the necessary corrective action immediately to bring the system into conformity, withdraw it, disable it or recall it, and to inform distributors and, where applicable, deployers, the authorised representative and importers. The authority's evaluation under Article 79(2) runs alongside these duties and does not replace them: operators must cooperate, and the authority may require corrective action within the shorter of 15 working days or the period in the relevant Union harmonisation legislation. Under Article 79(4) the operator must ensure corrective action across all affected systems, and if it fails to act, Article 79(5) provisional measures follow.
criteria_text: Both
Immediate corrective action required under Article 20(1) where system is non-compliant
Immediate investigation of causes is the provider's own duty under Article 20(2)
Investigation done in collaboration with reporting deployer where applicable, not deferred to market surveillance authority
criterion_remarks: The answer states the provider must both immediately investigate the causes and take corrective action, satisfying the 'both' criterion.
The answer cites Article 20(1) requiring immediate corrective action to bring the system into conformity, withdraw, disable, or recall it.
The answer explicitly states that the provider must immediately investigate the causes under Article 20(2), establishing it as the provider's own duty.
The answer specifies that investigation is done in collaboration with the reporting deployer where applicable, not deferred to the market surveillance authority.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with logically structured and grammatically complete prose suitable for regulatory compliance use.

rows.question: My local small language model says that, as a distributor of high-risk AI systems, I must be careful that transport conditions do not jeopardize compliance. But AI is just software, isn't it? So I am pretty sure my model hallucinated. What do you say?
rows.answer: The operator's model did not hallucinate. Under Article 24(3), distributors must ensure that, while a high-risk AI system is under their responsibility, storage or transport conditions do not jeopardise its compliance with the Section 2 requirements. The words "where applicable" limit this duty to cases where storage or transport can actually affect compliance. That typically happens when the AI system is built into, or supplied with, physical hardware such as sensors, devices or machinery, rather than delivered only as software.
criteria_text: No, not hallucinated
Article 24(3) applies
Duty applies only 'where applicable' (e.g., embedded/supplied hardware or physical media)
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly confirms the model did not hallucinate, aligning with the 'No, not hallucinated' criterion.
The answer cites and applies Article 24(3), stating the obligation it imposes on distributors.
The answer explains that the duty is limited by 'where applicable' and clarifies it applies when storage or transport conditions can affect compliance, such as with embedded or physical hardware.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: Does the AI Act prohibit or classifies as high-risk the use of AI in drones? Can I use AI in a drone to find who's around in town? And what if it's just a toy drone? And what about toy drones used for other applications?
rows.answer: The AI Act neither bans nor automatically classifies drones as high-risk; the rules depend on what the AI in the drone is intended to do. Using a drone to find out who is in town is generally prohibited under Article 5(1)(h) if it is real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement. The only exceptions are searching for abduction, trafficking or sexual-exploitation victims and missing persons (Article 5(1)(h)(i)), preventing a specific, imminent threat to life or a terrorist attack (Article 5(1)(h)(ii)), and locating suspects of serious Annex II offences (Article 5(1)(h)(iii)). Remote biometric identification outside that prohibition is high-risk under Article 6(2) and Annex III, point 1(a). A toy drone is a product under the Toy Safety Directive (Annex I, point 2). Under Article 6(1), its AI is high-risk only if it is a safety component of the toy, or the toy itself, and the toy must undergo third-party conformity assessment. A toy drone used for another purpose is classified by that purpose. For example, using it to identify people brings it under Article 5 or Annex III just like any other drone, whatever its toy form.
criteria_text: No blanket prohibition/high-risk classification for drones as such — turns on AI system's intended use under Article 6
Drone AI identifying people in public = remote biometric identification, high-risk under Annex III(1)(a), not the 1:1 verification exclusion
Toy status irrelevant — classification depends on intended use, not the device
Toy drone used for other application is high-risk only if that use matches Annex III (or Article 6(1) safety-component/conformity-assessment criteria)
criterion_remarks: States that classification depends on intended use under Article 6, not the drone itself.
Correctly identifies that identifying people in public constitutes remote biometric identification under Annex III(1)(a) and is high-risk, not falling under the 1:1 verification exclusion.
Explains that toy status does not determine classification—what matters is intended use, not the device type.
Clarifies that a toy drone used for another application is assessed based on that use, and gives an example tying it to the same rules as other drones.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents information in a logically ordered way suitable for regulatory guidance.

rows.question: We deployed a high-risk AI system in our company. We have a use in mind that is outside the intended use and our legal team say such a use is definitely no risk (no Annex I nor III apply). Can we just go ahead with the new use and do we need to keep logs for it?
rows.answer: No, you cannot simply go ahead, and you still need to keep the logs. As a deployer, Article 26(1) requires the operator to use the high-risk AI system in accordance with its instructions for use, so a use outside those instructions is not permitted without the provider's involvement. The operator's legal team's finding that the new use falls under neither route of Article 6 means the new purpose would not itself be high-risk. That covers Article 6(1), where the system is a safety component under Annex I legislation requiring third-party conformity assessment, and Article 6(2), where it is a use listed in Annex III. Because the new use is not high-risk, Article 25(1)(c) would not make you its provider. However, the Act does not allow a deployed high-risk system to lose that status for a single use. Under Article 26(6), the operator must keep the logs it automatically generates, to the extent they are under the operator's control, for a period appropriate to its intended purpose and of at least six months.
criteria_text: No, cannot proceed with the new use
Article 26(1) requires use in accordance with instructions for use; deviating from intended use is not excused merely because that use alone wouldn't trigger Annex III
Yes, logging duty under Article 26(6) still applies regardless of the particular use
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No, you cannot simply go ahead,' which matches the required verdict.

The answer explains that Article 26(1) requires use in accordance with instructions for use and that deviation is not permitted merely because the new use is not high-risk, capturing the substance of the criterion.
The answer affirms the ongoing logging obligation under Article 26(6) regardless of the new use, stating the duty applies based on the system's status and control over logs.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents a coherent regulatory analysis.

rows.question: Is AI software that helps clinicians take medical decisions around best treatment potentially high-risk? According to what Article and/or Annex?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as adopted, clinical treatment-decision software is normally high-risk under Article 6(1) read with Annex I, point 11 (Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices). Article 6(1) applies where two conditions are met: (a) the AI system is a product, or a safety component of a product, covered by that legislation, and (b) that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment. Software meant to support therapeutic decisions usually qualifies as a medical device, and the MDR typically requires a notified body to assess it. Annex III does not list clinical treatment support as such, so the Article 6(2) route and the Article 6(3) derogation do not decide the answer. The nearest Annex III items, points 5(a) and 5(d), cover public-authority eligibility for healthcare and emergency patient triage.
criteria_text: Yes
Article 6(2)
Annex III (healthcare access/provision)
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'Yes' as its opening word and affirms the system is high-risk, making the verdict unambiguous.

The answer attributes high-risk classification to Article 6(1), not Article 6(2) as required by the criterion. It explicitly distinguishes the Article 6(2) route from the correct basis, so it does not state the substance of the criterion.

The answer states that Annex III does not list clinical treatment support and that the nearest entries are different, directly contradicting the requirement to identify Annex III (healthcare access/provision) as the basis.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; avoids self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents a coherent regulatory analysis.

rows.question: About obligations of transparency to providers who want to use a GPAI model, do you need to disclose: date of release? number of paramaters? applicable model interaction with hardware? license? samples of outlier data used in training? Given clear yes/no to each item.
rows.answer: Under Article 53(1)(b) and Annex XII, the operator must disclose four of the five items to downstream providers, but not samples of outlier training data. Date of release: yes, together with methods of distribution (Annex XII.1(c)). Number of parameters: yes, together with the architecture (Annex XII.1(f)). How the model interacts with hardware or software outside the model: yes, where applicable (Annex XII.1(d)). Licence: yes (Annex XII.1(h)). Samples of outlier training data: no, because Annex XII.2(c) asks only for information on the type and provenance of the training, testing and validation data and the curation methods, and outlier detection appears only in Annex IV.2(d), which covers high-risk AI systems rather than GPAI models. This duty does not prejudice the protection of intellectual property and trade secrets, and under Article 53(2) it does not apply to free and open-source models with publicly available parameters unless the model has systemic risk.
criteria_text: Date of release - Yes
Architecture and number of parameters - Yes
Interaction with hardware or software - Yes
License - Yes
Samples of outlier training data - No
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that the date of release must be disclosed, aligning with the criterion.
The answer confirms disclosure of the number of parameters together with architecture, satisfying the substance of the criterion.
The answer affirms disclosure of model interaction with hardware or software, specifying it is required where applicable.
The answer clearly states that license information must be disclosed, matching the criterion.
The answer explicitly denies the obligation to disclose samples of outlier training data and explains why, referencing the correct annexes and provisions.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose with precise regulatory references; avoids self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Name the areas of high-risk use cases. Is healthcare decision making one of them?
rows.answer: No, healthcare decision-making is not one of the eight high-risk areas in Annex III, although some healthcare-related uses fall within them. Under Article 6(2), Annex III lists biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, access to essential private and public services and benefits, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control management, and administration of justice and democratic processes. Annex III(5) includes public authorities assessing eligibility for healthcare services, risk assessment and pricing for life and health insurance, and emergency healthcare patient triage. AI used in clinical decisions is high-risk under Article 6(1) instead if it is a medical device, or a safety component of one, under Annex I (Regulations (EU) 2017/745 and 2017/746) and needs third-party conformity assessment.
criteria_text: Biometrics; Critical infrastructure; Education and vocational training; Employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; Access to and enjoyment of essential private and public services and benefits; Law enforcement; Migration, asylum and border control management; Administration of justice and democratic processes
No
criterion_remarks: The answer lists all eight high-risk areas from Annex III, matching the substance of criterion 1.

The answer unambiguously states 'No' at the beginning and maintains that position, clarifying that while some healthcare-related uses are covered, healthcare decision-making as a general category is not one of the listed areas.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; avoids self-reference and presents information in a coherent, actionable manner.

rows.question: Could the introduction of guardrails in an AI agentic system reduce the risk of the system from high risk to moderate risk? What about changing the capabilities and intended use of the system?
rows.answer: No. Adding guardrails does not lower an agentic system from high-risk to "moderate" risk, and the Act has no moderate-risk tier. Under Article 6(2) with Annex III, high-risk status depends on the system's intended purpose in a listed use-case; under Article 6(1) with Annex I, it depends on the product route. The level of risk left after mitigation does not change that status. Guardrails count as risk-management and risk-control measures under Article 9(2) and help meet the Article 8 requirements, but they do not remove the classification. Changing the intended purpose or capabilities can change the classification if the system no longer falls within an Annex III use-case. It can also escape high-risk status under Article 6(3) if it poses no significant risk, for example because it performs a narrow procedural task or only a preparatory task. That exception never applies when the system profiles natural persons. Conversely, under Article 25(1)(c), anyone who changes the intended purpose so that a system becomes high-risk becomes its provider. Removing a use-case from Annex III itself requires a Commission delegated act under Article 7(3).
criteria_text: No - guardrails alone do not create an intermediate "moderate risk" tier; the Act's Article 6(3) derogation is binary (high-risk or exempted)

Exemption applies only where the system's intended task itself meets one of four Article 6(3) conditions: narrow procedural task; improving a previously completed human activity; detecting deviations from prior decisions without replacing human assessment; or a preparatory task
Yes - changing the system's capabilities/intended use can exit high-risk status if the redefined task now satisfies one of those conditions
Exception: an AI system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk, regardless of guardrails or intended-use changes
criterion_remarks: The answer states that the Act has no moderate-risk tier and that guardrails do not change high-risk status, affirming the binary nature of the classification under Article 6(3).

The answer identifies that exemption from high-risk status depends on the intended task meeting conditions such as narrow procedural task or preparatory task, reflecting the substance of Article 6(3)'s four conditions.
The answer confirms that changing the intended purpose or capabilities can change classification if the system no longer falls within an Annex III use-case or satisfies an Article 6(3) exemption.
The answer explicitly states that the exception for reduced risk does not apply when the system profiles natural persons, aligning with the mandatory high-risk designation in that case.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents regulatory analysis in a usable form.

rows.question: Is the use of deep-fake images in university classes to represent e.g. skin conditions in patients allowed? Does the artificial nature of the content need to be disclosed for such an evidently educational and illustrative use? If so, does the lighter transparency requirement apply like for certain law enforcement situations?
rows.answer: Yes, the use is allowed. No Article 5 prohibition covers generating illustrative medical images for teaching. Under Article 50(4), the university, as deployer, must disclose that a deep fake has been artificially generated or manipulated, and the Act gives no exemption for educational use. This applies to images that resemble real persons and would falsely appear authentic. The Article 50(2) duty on the AI provider to mark outputs in a machine-readable form applies separately. The only exemption, use authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, is a full exemption rather than a lighter one, and it does not apply to teaching. The lighter duty (disclosing in a way that does not hamper display or enjoyment) covers only "evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous" works, and the Act does not specify whether educational illustrations count as "analogous".
criteria_text: Yes, permitted
Disclosure still required under Article 50(4)
Lighter regime applies as "analogous work" to artistic/creative/fictional content — only existence of generated content must be disclosed, without hampering display/enjoyment
Law-enforcement carve-out is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and is inapplicable here
criterion_remarks: The answer states that the use is allowed and no prohibition under Article 5 applies, affirming permissibility.
The answer explicitly states that disclosure is required under Article 50(4) and confirms the obligation applies to the university as deployer.

The answer expresses uncertainty about whether educational illustrations qualify as 'analogous' to artistic or fictional works, failing to affirm that the lighter regime applies; it does not state the substance of the criterion.
The answer correctly identifies that the law-enforcement exemption is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and confirms it does not apply to teaching.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; avoids self-reference, hedging, or informality while clearly conveying regulatory analysis.

rows.question: A supermarket uses an AI tool that analyzes only current-cart and checkout anomalies (no biometrics, no face recognition, no sensitive-trait inference, no cross-context social scoring) to flag transactions for optional manual bag checks by store staff. The retailer claims this is "high risk like policing", as it: resembles investigation of potentially criminal offences (theft) + evaluates or classifies persons based on observed behaviour in a way that may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment. Is this situation potentially high-risk?
rows.answer: No, as described, this system is not high-risk, and it is not prohibited either. Under Article 6(2) and Annex III, the law-enforcement use-cases in Annex III point 6 only cover AI systems used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities. A private supermarket flagging carts for optional staff bag checks is not such an authority, so resembling the investigation of theft does not make it high-risk. The prohibition on social scoring in Article 5(1)(c) does not apply either. That ban requires evaluating or classifying people over a certain period of time based on social behaviour or personal or personality characteristics. The resulting score must also lead to detrimental treatment in unrelated social contexts or treatment that is unjustified or disproportionate. Analysing only the current cart and checkout anomalies for an optional check meets none of these conditions. Article 5(1)(d) does not apply either, because it targets risk assessments of criminal offending based solely on profiling or personality traits. These flags rest on objective transaction facts directly linked to the suspected theft.
criteria_text: No
Annex III.6 categories apply only where the AI system is used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities (or by Union institutions/bodies in support of law enforcement authorities)

A supermarket's own loss-prevention/bag-check tool, run by store staff, is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, so it falls outside Annex III.6 regardless of its resemblance to investigative or evaluative functions
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No' as the position, matching the required verdict.
The answer states that Annex III.6 applies only to systems used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities, conveying the substance of the criterion.
The answer explicitly explains that a supermarket's tool, run by store staff, is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, thus falling outside Annex III.6.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents reasoning in a logical, actionable manner.

rows.question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
rows.answer: No, you cannot skip the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements. The operator's AI system is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I, Section A, so it remains high-risk under Article 6(1), and Article 43(3) says the Section 2 requirements apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment. Article 43(3) also lets a manufacturer use a sectoral opt-out from third-party assessment only if it has applied harmonised standards, or where applicable the common specifications in Article 41, covering all Section 2 requirements. So the opt-out confirms the operator must meet those requirements; it does not exempt you from them.
criteria_text: No
Section 2 requirements still apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment (Art. 43(3), second sentence)
The third-party opt-out under sectoral legislation is available only if harmonised standards/common specifications applied cover ALL Section 2 requirements, not just the sectoral ones
